title: Private chef and household helper: who does what in the kitchen?
body_html:
When a private chef cooks in a home that already has a household helper, write down who does what in the kitchen before the first visit. A workable starting split: the chef decides the menu, cooks and makes food-handling calls; the helper keeps the household routines they already run. If you are still choosing a chef, begin with our private chef service in Dubai, then use this page to brief everyone at home.

Why a written split matters

Kitchens fail on small overlaps, not big ones: a helper tidies away a labelled container, a chef waits for a pan that is still being washed, or two people shop for the same ingredients. None of this is anyone's fault. It happens when nobody said who owns the task.

Treat the table below as a starting point and change any line that does not suit your household. It is a planning aid, not a service rule.

A suggested starting split

TaskSuggested ownerAgree in writing
Menu and recipesChef, within your briefDishes to avoid and any dietary rules
Grocery listChef writes itWho buys, who pays and who checks the delivery
Receiving and storing groceriesHelper or host, using the chef's listWhich shelves and fridge zones are the chef's
Prep and cookingChefWhether anyone else may stir, taste or move pots
Washing up during the visitDecide firstChef cleans as they go, helper washes, or both
Final clean of cooking areasDecide firstHob, counters, sink and floor, and who checks
Labelling cooked foodChefLabel style and reheating notes
Bins and recyclingHelperTiming, so food waste does not sit in the kitchen

Brief both people before day one

  1. Introduce them. A five-minute meeting in the kitchen beats a message passed on through you.
  2. Mark the chef's zones. Name the fridge shelf, pantry area and counter space that stay as the chef leaves them.
  3. Share one list. Give both people the allergy and dietary notes, written once, in one place.
  4. Agree the cleaning handover. Decide what counts as finished and who confirms it.
  5. Choose one contact. One person answers questions, so instructions do not conflict.

A worked example (hypothetical)

Imagine a family dinner on a Tuesday. The chef sends the grocery list on Monday. The helper receives the delivery and stores it in the zones you marked. The chef cooks, labels the extra portions and leaves a one-line reheating note. The helper washes the serving pieces and the chef wipes the hob and counters before leaving. This is an illustration of how the table works in an ordinary evening, not a fixed myCHEF procedure.

What to leave to the chef

  • Food handling and storage decisions for the food the chef cooks.
  • Whether a dish can be reheated, frozen or served cold.
  • Substitutions when an ingredient is missing. Ask the chef to tell you before changing anything that could affect an allergy.

Allergies and medical diets need instructions from your own qualified professional. Give them to the chef in writing rather than as a spoken reminder.

Next step

Write your own version of the table, share it with the chef and the helper, and review it after the first two visits. To plan a chef for your kitchen, see the private chef page, or start with the household menu brief guide.
